name: Flame
lede: Flame is a vivid reddish orange named for fire, though real flames are rarely this red, and in the pigment books the word names a black.

sections.title: Which flame
sections.body:
Paterson defines flame as a bright yellowish red, also called flame-red, and the swatch here fits that description [1]. It is a vivid reddish orange: ISCC-NBS filed it under that name in 1955, and Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 dates the name to 1590 [2]. The word was a colour term long before any standard chart caught up with it.

The name family is wide. Paterson lists flame-yellow, which he calls a bright orangey red, and flame pink, a dark orangey pink [1]. He also lists *flaming* for any intense colour and *fiery* for the look of fire, and notes that *flamboyant* once meant coloured in a flame-like manner [1]. The colour [[flame-scarlet|Flame Scarlet]] is a hotter, lighter neighbour, and the plainer [[orange]] and [[red-orange]] sit close by [2].

sections.title: Fire is not really red
sections.body:
Dictionaries commonly define red as the colour of fire or blood, Pastoureau notes, and fire is red in symbol and ritual almost everywhere [3]. Yet a real flame is rarely red. It is usually orange, yellow, sometimes blue or white, and even live coals lean toward orange [3]. A painter of flames therefore faces a mismatch between what symbolism asks for and what the eye sees.

Gurney, writing for painters, describes candlelight, lantern light and firelight as yellow-orange [4]. Such light is fairly weak and drops off quickly with distance from the flame, which is why objects close to it glow and the rest of a room goes dark [4]. A flame colour on a swatch is therefore a convention for fire, a bright and saturated version of what firelight does to a face.

Pastoureau also records that Romans watched the colour of their hearth fire for omens, and that very red flames, which were rare, were taken to herald important events [3]. The symbolism took the rare red flame as the real one.

sections.title: The red of hell and of Pentecost
sections.body:
Medieval art drew flames in red and the devil in black, the two colours of hell [5]. Pastoureau shows black and red together in scenes of damnation, red standing for the flames and the blood of the damned [5]. Pastoureau's history of green adds that the red-and-black devil gave way to a green one from about the mid-twelfth century, and that recipe collections tell painters to use a pigment called sandragon for devils' faces and infernal fire [6].

The same colour could be holy. In the Byzantine mosaic cycle at Hosios Loukas, the red flames of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost are set in white rays with a dark bluish-grey edge, a pattern also used for heavenly rays [7]. A twelfth-century account of the Holy Fire in Jerusalem calls the light unlike an ordinary flame and red like cinnabar [7]. Gage observes that the red there mattered less as a hue than as a sign of the finest sort of light [7].

sections.title: Flame colour in the ancient world
sections.body:
The Greek word *purron* meant flame colour, and the prefix *pyrrho-* still means reddish orange in English compounds, according to Paterson [1][8]. Plato claimed that leek green could be made by mixing purron with black, and Democritus thought pale green came from red and white [8][9]. Ball adds that purron was presumably an orange [8]. Plato defended the claim by saying that anyone who tried to verify it by experiment would forget the difference between human and divine nature [8].

Pliny described minium, the red lead pigment, as flame-coloured, according to St Clair, and the books record that minium was often confused with [[vermilion]] and cinnabar even though it is generally much yellower than either [9]. In both languages the word pointed at a region between yellow and red that had few other names [8][9].

sections.title: A black called flame
sections.body:
In the pigment books, *flame* names a black, not an orange. Flame carbons are carbons formed in the gas phase by the incomplete burning of hydrocarbons or wood, and the group includes lamp black, smoke black and the modern channel, furnace and thermal blacks [10]. The Compendium's entries for flame black and flame carbon simply send the reader to that group [10].

The tradition is old. Lamp black was made by burning oils, resins, rosin and pitch and collecting the soot on a cooler surface [10]. Coles describes the same operation: carbon deposited on a cold surface suspended over an oily flame [11]. Smoke black is the literal translation of the French *noir de fumée*, and one source, Watin in 1785, says it was gathered from burning pitch and tar [10]. Bistre, a brown ink, is a mixture of flame carbon, charred wood and tarry matter from burnt beechwood [10][11]. Heaton adds that gas black from coal gas was tried from about 1860 but proved too expensive [10].

So the word *flame* meets its own opposite. The fire that gave the orange its name also left the soot that gave painters black.

sections.title: Flame-coloured cloth
sections.body:
Cloth carried the name next. St Clair describes a portrait of William III, attributed to Thomas Murray, in which the king wears a cloak of flame-coloured velvet trimmed with ermine, an unmistakable nod to the House of Orange [12]. The Dutch took to the colour with enthusiasm in gratitude to William I, she writes, though the exact shade changed over the years [12].

Fiction used the same word for the same effect. In Mérimée's Carmen, the heroine's red skirt and shoes are fastened with flame-coloured ribbon, and Greenfield notes the outfit shocked Don José [13]. The fashion industry kept the habit: Garfield quotes a fashion-trade source who lists flame red and orange red among the many names for red [14].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive holds 23,781 paintings [15]. At least five per cent of the canvas lies within six units of this colour in 24 of them, as photographed, about one painting in a thousand [15]. A looser test, at least one per cent of the canvas within four units, finds 64 paintings, or 0.27 per cent [16]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not proof of any pigment or dye.

Flame is an accent colour. In 97 per cent of the 77 paintings where the within-painting lens finds it, it plays an accent against the painting's lightness order [16]. The strongest single hit is August Macke's [[painting:nga-121344|People by the Blue Lake]], 1913, where it covers 20 per cent of the canvas [15]. The place that most favours it is India: the colour is found in 11 of 721 Indian paintings, about 15 times the expected rate, and in six of 97 Rajput paintings [15][16]. A page of a Jaipur Ragamala set shows 18 per cent [[painting:aic-129883|a Jaipur Ragamala page]] [15].

The earliest match is [[painting:cma-125248|a panel by the Master of Rubielos de Mora]], dated 1400 [16]. That is more than five centuries before the 1955 ISCC-NBS record of the name, so it is a look-alike in an aged photograph and not evidence that the colour was named then [16]. In printed English the word *flame* peaks in the 1800s, but that count includes the literal fire and every other sense of the word [16].

questions.q: In the pigment books, what colour is a flame carbon?
True or false: Pliny called minium, red lead, flame-coloured.

openers: Real flames are rarely red; fire is red in symbols because symbols said so, not because the eye did.
In the pigment books flame means a black: flame carbon is soot, the fire's leftovers.
Next time you light a candle, look at the colour before you name it: yellow-orange, and it fades quickly as you step away.
